stage_name_raw: Dataset retrieval and benchmarking
stage_goal: retrieve and use standard evaluation datasets for benchmarking

evidence.text:
Datasets
We benchmark the models on three standard evaluation suites, all independently re-
trieved from the official websites. The definitions and background of the regression and classifi-
cation targets are introduced in the Appendix E.
• Materials Project (MP) Database: We use stable structures retrieved from the Materials Project
(Jain et al., 2020), comprising 122,959 entries with annotated formation energy, band gap, and
metal/non-metal classification labels. Additionally, 9,473 of these entries include mechanical
properties such as bulk modulus, shear modulus and Young’s modulus. The dataset is managed
using the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE), and is available at https://huggingface.
co/datasets/caobin/CPPbenchmark.
• JARVIS-DFT (dft_3d): This dataset contains 75,993 entries, each annotated with formation
energy, band gap (calculated using either the OptB88vDW functional, denoted as OPT, or the
TBMBJ functional, denoted as MBJ), bulk modulus, shear modulus, total energy (calculated us-
ing the OptB88vDW functional), and energy above the hull (Ehull ) (Choudhary et al., 2020).
We also evaluate the baselines on the JARVIS-DFT-3D-2021 dataset (55,723 entries), which
serves as an important supplementary benchmark.
• Matbench (MB) Suite: We evaluate the models on several tasks from the Matbench suite (Dunn
et al., 2020): matbench_jdft2d (636 entries; exfoliation energy), matbench_mp_e_form
(132,752 entries; formation energy), matbench_log_gvrh (10,987 entries; shear modulus),
and matbench_dielectric (4,764 entries; refractive index).

stage_name_raw: Crystal structure representation and graph construction
stage_goal: represent crystal structures as graphs with node and edge features

evidence.text:
Crystal Structures
Crystal structures can be described using a fundamental unit, such as a prim-
itive cell, conventional unit cell, Bravais lattice, or asymmetric unit, together with its associated
atoms.
The unit is defined by a 3 × 3 lattice matrix that specifies its geometry in real space.
Formally, a crystal structure is represented as M = (A, P, L), where A denotes atomic types,
P = [p1, . . . , pN] ∈R3×N contains the fractional or Cartesian coordinates of the N atoms, and
L = [l1, l2, l3] ∈R3×3 defines the periodic lattice in real space.

Graph embedding
A crystal structure is represented as a graph G = (V, E), where vertices V =
{v1, v2, . . . , vN} correspond to atoms one-hot encoded attributes (Xie & Grossman, 2018) and
edges E ⊆V × V encode atomic interactions within a cutoff radius. Each atom i is characterized
by a node feature h(0)
i
= Embed(vi) ∈Rd and coordinates ri = (xi, yi, zi) ∈R3. Edge features
between atoms i and j are defined as:
eij = RBF(dij) ⊕SBF(θijk) ⊕dij,
dij = ∥ri −rj∥,
(6)
where RBF(·) denotes a radial basis function, SBF(·) a spherical basis function (Gasteiger et al.),
θijk is the angle between bond ij and bond ik, and ⊕indicates concatenation.

stage_goal: train PRDNet to integrate graph embeddings and learned pseudo-particle diffraction while enforcing E(3)-invariance

evidence.text:
Multi-Modal Feature Fusion
The integration of graph-based crystal real-space features h(L)
i
and
physics-based diffraction representations Fconcat is achieved through a fusion mechanism:
g = GlobalPool({h(L)
i

i=1),

zfused = MLPfusion([g ⊕d]).
(7)
GlobalPool(·) aggregates node features across the entire crystal structure, MLPdiff(·) maps physics-
based descriptors to the embedding space, and MLPfusion(·) produces the final fused representation.

Model Invariance
Crystals are inherently symmetrical. Following existing work (Yan et al., 2024;
Liu et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024), we force the model prediction to be invariant to E(3) group
(i.e., the rotation, reflection, and translation of input crystals). Specifically, according to Eq. 7, the
final representation output zfused depends on the g and d. Since g depends on the relative geometric
features dij and θijk (Eq.6) that remain unchanged under E(3) operations, g is E(3)-invariant.
Consequently, because d is also E(3)-invariant, the model output is E(3)-invariant, as shown in
Section 4.3.

To accommodate the diverse nature of crystal property prediction tasks and improve training stabil-
ity, PRDNet employs Huber loss (Meyer, 2021) for training.
The Huber loss combines the advantages of L2 loss for small errors and L1 loss for large errors:

stage_name_raw: Quantitative evaluation on benchmark datasets
stage_goal: assess PRDNet performance against baselines using MAE and accuracy metrics

evidence.text:
5.1
RESULTS
Benchmarks Performance
Across the MP, JARVIS-DFT, and Matbench benchmarks, PRDNet
consistently delivers superior or competitive performance compared with existing models. On the
MP dataset (Table 1), PRDNet surpasses all baselines, achieving the lowest errors in formation en-
ergy (0.028 eV/atom), band gap (0.151 eV), bulk modulus (0.035 log(GPa)), shear modulus (0.108
log(GPa)), and Young’s modulus (0.104 log(GPa)), while also reaching the highest metal/non-metal
classification accuracy (93.3%).

stage_name_raw: Ablation study to validate architectural components
stage_goal: isolate contributions of individual modules (diffraction, attention, residuals, edge features)

evidence.text:
Ablation Study
To validate the effectiveness of each component in the PRDNet architecture, we
perform systematic ablation studies that isolate the contributions of individual modules and design
choices. We evaluate PRDNet across diverse property prediction tasks using the Materials Project,
JARVIS-DFT and Matbench databases, ensuring a comprehensive assessment. Table 3 presents the
ablation results on the MP dataset, while Appendix B, Table 5, and Table 6 report the results on
JARVIS-DFT and Matbench, respectively. The results show that each component is essential for
optimal performance. Removing the diffraction module causes the obversely performance drop,
underscoring its critical role. Likewise, using single-head attention, removing residual connections,
or excluding edge features consistently degrades performance, indicating that multi-head attention,
residual updates, and edge features collectively strengthen representation learning. These findings
confirm the effectiveness of our default architecture, in which all modules work synergistically to
achieve the highest accuracy across material property predictions.

The dielectric tensor is symmetric under the permutation of Cartesian indices, εij = εji, and therefore admits the decomposition εij = Tαβ Y α 1 Y β 1 = ε(0)  ε(2) = Σ‘∈{0, 2} Σ‘ m = −‘ εm (‘) Y m ‘ , (1) which separates the scalar trace component (l= 0) from the traceless symmetric tensor component (l= 2).
This approach transforms the tensors from the Cartesian basis into the spherical-harmonics basis, making it easier to work with tensor properties in systems with rotational and inversion symmetries.

stage_name_raw: Clean and filter WBM test set by protostructure matching
stage_goal: Remove potential data leakage between MP training set and WBM test set by eliminating structures with matching final protostructures.
stage_output: cleaned WBM unique prototype test set of 215,488 structures

evidence.text: To control for the potential adverse effects of leakage between the MP training set and the WBM test set, we cleaned the WBM test set based on protostructure matching. We refer to the combination of a materials prototype and the elemental assignment of its wyckoff positions as a protostructure following ref. 62. First we removed 524 pathological structures in WBM based on formation energies being larger than 5 eV per atom or smaller than −5 eV per atom. We then removed from the WBM test set all examples where the final protostructure of a WBM material matched the final protostructure of an MP material. In total, 11,175 materials were cleaned using this filter. We further removed all duplicated protostructures within WBM, keeping the lowest energy structure in each instance, leaving 215,488 structures in the unique prototype test set.

stage_name_raw: crystal structure representation
stage_goal: represent crystal materials as structured inputs (A, X, L)

evidence.text: Crystal materials can be viewed as a 3D point cloud (Fig. 4(a)) of atoms arranged in an orderly repeating pattern. For a material with N atoms in its unit cell, the structure can be defined as M = (A, X, L). Atom Type Matrix: A = [a1, a2, ..., aN]T ∈RN×k, where each ai is a one-hot vector denoting the atomic type of the ith atom, and k is the maximum number of possible atom types. Coordinate Matrix: X = [x1, x2, ..., xN]T ∈RN×3, where xi ∈R3 represents the 3D coordinates of the ith atom in the unit cell. Lattice Matrix: L = [l1, l2, l3]T ∈R3×3, which specifies how the unit cell repeats itself in 3D space along directions l1, l2, and l3 to form the periodic crystal.

The encoder module takes the crystal material M = (A, X, L) as input and encodes atomic types, coordinates and lattice structure into the latent space: Z = Eφ(A, X, L)

The network takes as input the intermediate noisy latent Zt along with the time step t and predicts the corresponding clean latent representation as:  ̄Z1 = Fθ(Zt, t).

evidence.text:
3.4 Molecular Dynamics of Small Molecules
We evaluate Orb on the MD17-10k benchmark, following the protocol of [33]. This benchmark assesses the quality of NVT Molecular Dynamics (MD) trajectories generated by machine learning models on four small organic molecules (aspirin, ethanol, naphthalene, and salicylic acid) using two key metrics:
• Stability: the number of picoseconds until the system “collapses” / “breaks apart”, which is detected via large deviations in the interatomic distances compared to those of a ground-truth ab initio trajectory. 300 ps is the length of the simulation and thus the maximum possible stability.
• “h(r)”: a 1-Wasserstein metric on the distributions of interatomic distances present in the model-trajectory vs those present in the ab initio trajectory.
In addition to these two metrics, we report a test set Force MAE (meV/ ̊A).

stage_name_raw: sequencing lignin monomers and conditional linkage generation
stage_goal: To generate all possible monomer sequences and linkage arrangements consistent with experimental S/G ratios, bond ratios, and degree of polymerization.

evidence.text:
Sequencing lignin monomers and conditional linkage generation.
Phenyl propane units (Fig. 2) form the core backbone of the lignin structure42. The base unit in the backbone contains structural features of p-coumaryl alcohol (H), in which an allylic alcohol moiety is connected to the para position of phenolic ring. The three carbon atoms present in the aliphatic side chain are located at α, β and γ positions respectively. During lignin structure generation, the H monomer is considered as the base unit whereas coniferyl alcohol (G monomer) and syringyl alcohol (S monomer) are modifications of the base unit with additions of one (position 3) and two (position 3 and 5) methoxy groups, respectively.
The sequence generation code implements Heap’s permutation algorithm43 using a recursive function adjusted to generate all possible permutations of n monomer units (Fig. 3).

stage_name_raw: generation of topological matrices and molecular graph representations
stage_goal: To convert monomer sequences and linkage patterns into directed molecular graphs encoded as adjacency and connectivity matrices.

evidence.text:
Generation of topological matrices and molecular graph representations.
The structure generation mimics the monomer sequencing in chain-growth polymerization by assigning probabilities to the presence of specific monomer pairs. Resulting molecular structures can be represented as graphs where nodes represent monomer units, and the edges correspond to covalent bonds formed during the polymerization process.

Molecular graphs can be efficiently represented in tabular form as a pair of topological matrices46 that define the relationship between monomer units. The information in the topological matrices includes linkages (i.e., adjacency matrix) and bond types (i.e., connectivity matrix).

stage_name_raw: generation of molecular structures and consistency validation
stage_goal: To convert molecular graphs into canonical SMILES representations and validate structural correctness and consistency with input constraints.

evidence.text:
Generation of molecular structures and consistency validation.
The molecular structure of a lignin is represented using the canonical SMILES (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System) notation which represents the molecular structure in a string format47. Directed graphs are converted to canonical SMILES by generating the monomer molecular graph and mapping the respective linkages using the Chemistry Development Toolkit (CDK)48, a widely used open-source cheminformatics toolkit.

Finally, generated structures are checked for the acceptance criteria that include structures with unique and valid SMILES representation; and number of nodes matching the requested degree of polymerization.

evidence.text: A detailed comparative analysis was performed to ensure that the properties of the generated lignin structures are consistent with experimental values reported in the literature. To this end, the structure of the generated polymers (e.g., bond compositions, functional groups, and end groups) were compared with properties derived from experimental observations for MWL from Spruce and Birch wood.
Additional validation was performed by comparing the structures in the LGS dataset with structures generated using the Lignin-KMC model20.

evidence.text:
File format.
The LGS dataset provides lignin structures in three different formats to facilitate the compatibility with a variety of computational chemistry software platforms (e.g., ADF49, Avogadro50) and data analytics tools:
• 
Application specific files: Molecular data files (MOL), which is a widely used chemical structure file format supported by most software packages for molecular dynamics. The data file contains 3D conformation of the generated molecule, which can be used in molecular editors such as Avogadro to visualize and analyze the spatial arrangements.
• 
Tabular files: Text files using the Comma Separated Value (CSV) format that represent each molecular graph using connectivity and adjacency matrices.
• 
Key/value file: Text files using the JavaScript Object Notation (JSON51) format that provide comprehensive information that includes the definition of molecular structures using SMILES together with properties such as molecular weight, functional group counts and bond ratios.

stage_name_raw: Calculation of relative sound velocities and elastic constants

stage_name_raw: Selection and comparison of theoretical model predictions

Predictions for the porosity dependence of the sound velocity22 can be derived from the well-known predictive models for elastic properties, including the Maxwell–Mori–Tanaka (MMT) relation,23,24 the differential relation24,25 or Gibson–Ashby relation for open-cell foams,26,27 the (Pabst–Gregorová-type) exponential relation28,29 and the self-consistent model relation,24,29 as well as the numerical (Pabst–Uhlířová) benchmark relation for partially sintered materials with concave porosity (overlapping solid sphere model)30 and the one-parameter (Pabst–Gregorová) percolation relation,31

stage_name_raw: Powder Preparation
stage_goal: Prepare homogeneous mixture of starting powders for sintering.

evidence.text: The initial powders were mixtures of α-Si3N4 (SN-E10, UBE Industries Ltd., Japan), MnO (purity > 99.9%, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., China), and Al2O3 (purity > 99.9%, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., China). stage_name_raw: Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS)

The sintering process was conducted using the SPS method (SPS-725, Fuji Electronic Industrial Co., Ltd., Japan) with a constant heating rate of 100◦C/min. To investigate the densification behavior, the processing envelope included sintering temperatures ranging from 1400◦C to 1700◦C, uniaxial pressures between 100 and 150 MPa, and holding times spanning 5 to 20 min.

stage_name_raw: Characterizations
stage_goal: Quantify density, phase composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties of sintered samples.

evidence.text: The density of the sintered samples was determined via the Archimedes principle. Mechanical properties, including Vickers hardness and fracture toughness, were evaluated using a Vickers hardness tester (TH700, Beijing TIME High Technology Ltd., China).

stage_name_raw: Densification Analysis
stage_goal: Screen sintering conditions that achieve near-theoretical densification at low temperature.
stage_input: density and relative density data from Table 1
stage_output: optimal sintering condition: 1450°C achieving 97% relative density

evidence.text: Near-theoretical densification was achieved at a relatively low temperature of 1450◦C, demonstrating the strong fluxing effect of MnO in promoting liquid-phase-assisted sintering.

However, increasing the temperature from 1400◦C to 1450◦C significantly improved density; for instance, density increased from 2.85 g/cm3 (RD = 87%) in the 1400-100-5 sample to 3.02 g/cm3 (RD = 92%) in the 1450-100-5 sample. Furthermore, at this temperature, the density of the samples increased with the extension of holding time, such as the density of 1450-100-20 sample (3.18 g/cm3 , RD = 97%) was noticeably higher than that of 1450-100-5 sample (3.02 g/cm3 , RD = 92%).

stage_name_raw: Phase Transformation and Microstructure Screening
stage_goal: Screen sintering conditions that enable continuous tuning of α/β phase ratio and associated microstructural evolution.
stage_output: tunable α/β phase ratio (e.g., 10% to 100% β-Si3N4)
microstructural transition from equiaxed α-grains to elongated β-grains

evidence.text: The α–β phase transformation was found to be highly sensitive to the sintering conditions, enabling continuous tuning of the α/ β phase ratio over a wide range. This controlled phase transformation resulted in pronounced microstructural changes, from fine equiaxed α- Si3 N4 grains to elongated columnar β-Si3 N4 grains, leading to a broad and tunable hardness-fracture toughness range.

By adjusting sintering parameters, the β-phase content can be flexibly controlled. Under a constant holding time of 20 min, the β-Si3N4 content increases significantly from 50% in the 1600-100-20 sample to 100% in the 1700-100-20 sample. At a constant temperature of 1600◦C, extending the holding time from 5 to 20 min raised the β-Si3N4 content from 10% in the 1600-100-5 sample to 50% in the 1600-100-20 sample.

stage_name_raw: Mechanical Properties Correlation
stage_goal: Validate the correlation between phase/microstructure and mechanical performance.
stage_input: hardness and fracture toughness data (Table 1, Table 3, Figure 7)
stage_output: confirmed structure–property relationships: fine α-grains → high hardness; elongated β-grains → high fracture toughness

evidence.text: The high hardness at lower temperatures is primarily attributed to the high content of α-Si3N4 phase and the refined equiaxed grain structure. The significant increase in fracture toughness when temperature rises or holding time extends is attributed to the increased content of β-Si3N4.
The highest hardness of 23.6 ± 0.4 GPa was obtained in the 1550-100-5 sample, while the highest fracture toughness of 8.4 ± 0.4 MPa ⋅m1/2 was achieved in the 1700-100-20 sample.

stage_name_raw: Grafting silane coupling agents onto SiO2 surface

stage_name_raw: Constructing and optimizing periodic PI/SiO2 composite models

stage_output: optimized PI/SiO2 composite models for each functional group

stage_name_raw: Simulating and quantifying structural, dynamic, and property metrics

evidence.text: The results showed that the interface structure with PhCOOH simultaneously elevated the static dielectric permittivity (εs) and Young modulus of the PI-based composites. Due to enhanced intrinsic polarization of the SiO2 particles and the interface polarization in the composites, the εs of PIS-PhCOOH composites (6.66) was 28% higher than that of PIS (5.21). stage_name_raw: synchrotron X-ray computed tomography during in-situ tensile loading

stage_name_raw: 3D reconstruction and volume registration
stage_goal: Reconstruct projection data into aligned 3D volumes and register them to eliminate rigid-body motion between loading steps.
stage_output: registered, overlaid 3D volumes for each material

evidence.text: The reconstruction of the projection into 3D volumes was done using a filtered back-projection algorithm provided by SLS.

For each material, four of the volumes were selected, corresponding to the steps with ∼0, 40, 73, and 95% of the failure load, and presented in the current study. Using the Avizo 2019.3 software, the volumes of each material were registered (overlaid) on each other via 3D rigid transform and with “Normalized Mutual Information” and resampled with “Standard” (linear) interpolation. This eliminates the rigid body motion and rotation occurred during loading and allows easily locating the VOIs.

stage_name_raw: volume of interest (VOI) cropping and coordinate alignment
stage_goal: Extract representative subvolumes from the registered 3D data and align their coordinate system with the laminate geometry.

evidence.text: A volume of interest in the middle 0 ° ply is chosen and located in the 3D image of each loading step ( Fig. 1 ). The cropped volumes of interest for each material are presented in this publication...

A VOI of 420 × 1030 × 450 μm 3 ( x, y, z ) for the glass/epoxy and of 390 × 830 × 440 μm 3 ( x, y, z ) for the carbon/epoxy material was chosen in their middle 0 ° plies (the blue box in Fig. 1 a and b, respectively) and cropped from the larger volumes.

The volumes were slightly ( < 10 °) rotated, using bicubic interpolation in MATLAB, so that the image coordinate system equals the laminate coordinate system: z - and y -axes are aligned respectively with the nominal 0 ° and 90 ° lamina directions, and x -axis is normal to the laminate plane ( Fig. 1 ).

stage_name_raw: Long-term stability and electronic property validation
stage_goal: To confirm stability of Pt SAs under continuous illumination and correlate photocatalytic performance with TiO2 electronic quality (conductivity, defect states).
stage_output: evidence that Sn diffusion degrades performance at >450 °C

evidence.text: Importantly, long-term stability tests (Figure S1d, Supporting Information) confirm that the hydrogen evolution performance remains stable for continuous illumination, despite partial aggregation of Pt single atoms into nanoparticles.

This trend further supports that Pt SA density is not the dominant factor in determining catalytic efficiency. The hydrogen evolution rate reaches a maximum at 450 °C, even though Pt loading is slightly higher at 800 °C. Instead, the results strongly suggest that the electronic quality of the TiO2 film—especially its conductivity and defect properties—is the primary parameter controlling performance.

To analyze the inuence of the high-entropy effect on the microstructure of the matrix, we employed transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) to observe the detailed structural features in Pb0.875Sn0.125Se0.5Te0.25S0.25-2at%Cu.

stage_name_raw: First-principles electronic band structure calculations
stage_goal: Validate the entropy-driven band structure modifications (e.g., increased band degeneracy, reduced band gap, enhanced DOS near Fermi level) that underpin improved Seebeck coefficient.
stage_output: quantified band gap (Eg) reduction and increased DOS near Fermi level

evidence.text: Here, we performed rst-principles density functional theory calculations, as shown in Fig. 9. Fig. 9a and b demonstrate the established unit cell structures of low-entropy PbSe and high-entropy PbSe. As shown in Fig. 9c and d, a large number of impurity bands appeared in the conduction and valence bands due to the introduction of Se/Te/Sn. Multiple energy bands pushed the peak of the band toward the Fermi level, reducing an energy difference between different energy valleys and enhancing the band degeneracy NV. The band gap (Eg) decreased, which is consistent with the experimental results of the optical band gap (Fig. S2†). As shown in Fig. 9e, the high-entropy sample exhibited a signicant increase in the DOS near the Fermi level compared with the low-entropy sample...

Consequently, the thermoelectric properties of Pb0.875Sn0.125Se0.5Te0.25S0.25−2at%Cu are remarkably improved, with a maximum dimensionless merit ZTmax of ∼1.46 at 623 K and an average dimensionless merit ZTave of ∼1.15 at 300–700 K. stage_name_raw: Fiber surface characterization using SEM
stage_goal: To examine and compare the surface topology of IM and HM carbon fibers.
stage_output: SEM images revealing longitudinal grooves on IM fiber surfaces and smoother surfaces on HM fiber surfaces

evidence.text: To investigate the microstructure of IM and HM fibers as a potential factor affecting the interface shear-strength measurements, the fiber surface was characterized using SEM.

Figure 2a,b shows well-defined longitudinal grooves on the surfaces of the IM fiber. Unlike the ridged surface of the IM fibers, reflecting the structure of the polymeric precursor caused by the wet spinning process during carbon fiber manufacturing, HM fibers have a relatively smooth surface and longitudinal grooves are less noticeable, as shown in Figure 2c,d.

stage_name_raw: Hypothesis generation on interface friction mechanism
stage_goal: To propose that surface topology differences (roughness) cause higher interface friction for IM fibers, thereby improving interface strength.
stage_input: Literature on surface roughness and interfacial friction [26–29]
stage_output: Hypothesis: IM fiber surface roughness increases interfacial friction, contributing to higher interface shear strength

evidence.text: Surface roughness can significantly affect fiber–matrix interface behavior. Schadler et al. [26] recognized roughness as the most important factor for improving the interfacial shear strength of carbon-fiber–thermoplastic composites. Surface roughness of the fiber can increase interfacial friction by improving micromechanical bonding (interlocking) of the fiber and matrix surfaces that are in contact.

In particular, differences in the surface topology may cause much higher interface friction for IM carbon fibers compared to the HM fibers, which is responsible for the interface strength improvement.

stage_name_raw: In situ SEM-based fiber push-out and push-back experiments
stage_goal: To quantitatively measure interface shear strength (IFSS) and interface friction strength for IM and HM fibers in the hybrid CFRP.
stage_input: Hybrid CFRP thin membrane specimen (23 μm thick)
Micromechanical load frame integrated with SEM

evidence.text: In this work, in situ SEM-based fiber push-out and push-back tests are utilized for a hybrid CFRP to measure HM and IM carbon-fiber–polymer-matrix interface shear strength and interface friction strength, respectively.
The force applied on the fiber leads to fiber–matrix interface debonding until the fiber completely loses its load-carrying capacity and protrudes from the opposite sample surface.

By measuring the maximum applied load Pmax during the push-back test, the thickness of the specimen h, and the fiber radius r, the fiber–matrix interface friction strength can be calculated using Equation (1).

stage_name_raw: Comparison and statistical analysis of IFSS and interface friction strength
stage_goal: To quantify and statistically compare interface shear strength and interface friction strength between IM and HM fibers.
stage_input: Interface friction strength measurements from push-back tests
stage_output: Average interface friction strength: 36.7 MPa (IM) vs. 18.9 MPa (HM)
48% higher interface friction for IM fibers

evidence.text: Figure 7a confirms that the average measured IFSS value in IM fibers (122 Mpa) is 30% higher than HM fibers (93 Mpa).

According to the outcome of the fiber push-back tests, the average interfacial friction strength of HM fibers was estimated as 18.9 MPa while IM fibers in the same material system have an average interfacial friction strength of 36.7 MPa. The test results show an approximately 48% decrease in the average values of the fiber-to-matrix interface friction strength for the HM carbon fibers compared to their IM counterparts.

stage_name_raw: Correlation of surface topology with mechanical measurements
stage_goal: To link observed surface topography differences (grooved vs. smooth) to the measured 48% difference in interface friction and its contribution to the 29 MPa IFSS difference.
stage_input: Quantified interface friction and IFSS values
stage_output: Mechanistic explanation: Surface roughness of IM fibers increases micromechanical interlocking and interfacial friction, contributing substantially to interface shear strength

evidence.text: The 18 MPa difference in the interface friction between IM and HM fibers appears to have a major contribution to the 29 MPa IFSS difference between IM and HM fibers. In particular, a substantial difference in fiber surface topology, as illustrated in Figure 2, with IM fibers exhibiting much more surface roughness compared to HM fibers, is likely to be an underlying cause.
Such experiments reveal an approximately 48% higher maximum shear traction due to interface friction for IM carbon fibers compared to HM fibers.

stage_name_raw: Building initial MPE chain structures with functional groups
stage_goal: Construct atomistic models of modified polyethylene chains containing keto, ester, or amide functional groups evenly distributed at a functional-group-to-ethylene-unit ratio of 0.04.
stage_input: polyethylene chain with 100 ethylene repeating units
keto, ester, or amide functional groups

evidence.text: The initial structures of MPE chains were built using Avogadro software.31 The polyethylene chain contains 100 ethylene repeating units, sufficient to establish intermolecular entangle- ments. MPE chains contain different in-chain functional groups, with the ratio between ethylene groups and functional groups set at 0.04, and the functional groups evenly distributed (see Figure S1).

stage_name_raw: Equilibrating semicrystalline MPE systems via MD simulation
stage_goal: Generate equilibrated semicrystalline structures of MPE systems by energy minimization, heating, controlled cooling, and final equilibration to confirm thermodynamic equilibrium before mechanical testing.

evidence.text: Initially, a single MPE chain was energy minimized and then equilibrated in a vacuum at 300 K in the isothermal (NVT) ensemble within a cubic box of 100 Å for 100 ps. Subsequently, we randomly packed 316 MPE chains into a simulation box of 200 Å. After energy minimization to adjust atomic coordinates, the systems were equilibrated at 500 K for 100 ns and then cooled at a rate of 0.5 K/ns from 500 to 300 K. Final equilibration was performed at 300 K for 100 ns. Equilibrium was confirmed by monitoring the convergence of key system observables—namely the total potential energy, density, radius of gyration and crystallinity —over the final 100 ns of equilibration.

stage_name_raw: Performing uniaxial tensile deformation simulations
stage_goal: Obtain stress–strain relationships and quantify mechanical properties (modulus, yield stress, ultimate tensile strength, toughness) under deformation.
stage_output: mechanical property metrics (yield stress, modulus, ultimate tensile strength, toughness)

evidence.text: Once we achieved an equilibrated semicrystalline system, we conducted uniaxial tensile deformation simulations at 300 K using a strain rate of 8 × 107 s−1 to balance accuracy and efficiency while considering computational feasibility (see Note 1).18
To explore the mechanical response of the polymer systems (see Note 1), uniaxial tensile stress−strain relationships were obtained through MD simulations (see Figure 1 A,B).

stage_name_raw: Performing DFT calculations to analyze intermolecular interactions and binding energies
stage_goal: Quantify and compare the strength and nature of intermolecular interactions (especially hydrogen bonding) among MPE systems using electronic-structure calculations.

stage_name_raw: Analysis of recrystallization mechanisms
stage_goal: To identify and distinguish the dominant recrystallization mechanisms (DDRX, CDRX, SRX) and their dependence on deformation parameters.

evidence.text: The main mechanism of DRX is discontinuous DRX (DDRX). The continuous DRX (CDRX) is less occurring. Static recrystallization (SRX) occurs during the isothermal holding time between deformation passes.

When the segregated phase particles are distributed in bands, the static recrystallization (SRX) grains will produce microstructures with approximate orientations of incomplete recrystallization due to the particle-stimulated nucleation (PSN) mechanism.

stage_name_raw: Correlation of microstructural evolution with deformation parameters

evidence.text: The increase in deformation temperature contributes significantly to dynamic recrystallization (DRX), and the main mechanism of DRX is discontinuous DRX (DDRX). The continuous DRX (CDRX) is less occurring. Static recrystallization (SRX) occurs during the isothermal holding time between deformation passes. SRX becomes more and more apparent with temperature and the holding time.
The effect of 1200 °C/30 min and 1200 °C/10 min process parameters on the microstructure of the alloy is mainly reflected in the difference in the SRX degree during the isothermal holding period.

The MaScQA benchmark1 addresses this gap by providing a curated dataset of 650 questions covering diverse sub-elds within materials science, including thermodynamics, atomic structure, mechanical behavior, and materials characterization.

stage_name_raw: pretraining dataset construction (R2CID)

evidence.text: Our pretraining dataset, designated R2CID, integrates three distinct components: scientific literature from materials research publications, a curated subset of RedPajama (the original pretraining corpus for LLaMA models), and crystallographic information files (CIF).

stage_name_raw: continued pretraining (CPT)

evidence.text: The initial stage comprised continued pretraining (CPT) on the base LLaMA models with an extensive and meticulously curated corpus developed in-house, namely R2CID... with greater than 30 billion tokens of MatSci knowledge, encompassing approximately 4 million peer-reviewed publications (94.43%), crystallographic information files (2.499%), and MatSci community discourse (0.019%). Additionally, we incorporated a strategic 3% subset of RedPajama data... to preserve fundamental linguistic capabilities while concurrently mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

stage_name_raw: parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) for generation

stage_output: LLaMat-CIF models capable of unconditional crystal structure generation

evidence.text: Following this, parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) was employed on LLaMat-CIF to enable crystal generation, a task of importance in materials discovery (see Methods Sec.4 for details).

stage_name_raw: quantitative assessment of crystal generation
stage_goal: Evaluate the quality and novelty of the generated crystal structures using established metrics.

evidence.text:
To evaluate the performance of LLMs for crystal generation, we rely on the following metrics.
1. Validity check: Structural validity and compositional validity are calculated as described in [39]. The former indicates that the distance between the centres of two atoms is greater than the sum of their atomic radii. The compositional validity is obtained using SMACT[60], which identifies if the given material is charge neutral based on all possible charge combinations.
2. Coverage: We use two coverage metrics, COV-R (recall) and COV-P (precision), described in [39] to measure the similarity between ensembles of generated materials and ground truth materials in the test set.
3. Property statistics: We compute the Wasserstein distance between the property distributions of the generated materials and the test materials.
4. Stability Check: We used M3GNet ([61]) to approximate force, energy, and stress in crystal unit cells.

stage_name_raw: Alloy composition design targeting oxygen-mediated <c + a> slip activation and β-phase-mediated slip transfer
stage_goal: Design Ti–O–Fe compositions satisfying oxygen threshold (≥0.40% O) for <c + a> slip activation and Fe content (~4% Fe) to achieve ~20 vol.% β-phase for slip transfer mediation.
stage_input: oxygen threshold for <c + a> activation (≥0.40% O)
JMatPro thermodynamic predictions for β-phase fraction
empirical data on α/β lath thickness ratio in additively manufactured Ti-6Al-4V

evidence.text: According to our alloy design principle, the oxygen content in the α-Ti phase must be > 0.4% to fully activate the <c + a> slip system48. However, excessive oxygen may still lead to premature failure of the alloy50. Therefore, we choose a total addition of 0.45% O.

Similarly, according to our alloy design principle, it is crucial to introduce an appropriate amount of β phase as a mediator to promote extensive slip transfer of dislocations across multiple α−β interfaces. Based on JMatPro 7.0 predictions, under equilibrium conditions, the addition of 4% Fe is expected to produce about 20 vol.% β phase at RT. Therefore, our alloy composition is determined to be Ti-0.45O-4Fe.
To further validate our design framework, we increased the O content from 0.45% to 0.50% and the Fe content from 4% to 5% according to our design criteria, targeting the Ti–0.5O–5Fe composition.

stage_name_raw: Production of gas-atomized spherical Ti-O-Fe powder
stage_goal: Acquire feedstock powder with precise composition and suitable particle size distribution for PBF-LB processing.
stage_input: Ti sponge, Ti-32Fe master alloy block, TiO2 powder

evidence.text:
Powder production
First, Ti-0.45O-4Fe alloy ingots were prepared by triple vacuum arc consumable melting using titanium sponge, Ti-32Fe master alloy block and TiO2 powder in a mass ratio of 86.5:12.5:1. The ingots were subsequently forged at1100 °C into round barsmeasuring φ60 × 600 mm. These bars were then gas-atomized into powder using an electrode induction gas atomization (EIGA) system.

The produced powders had a normal size distribution (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b) and were sieved to a size range of 20-50 μm for the PBF-LB process, with characteristic diameters of Dv(10) = 21.7 μm, Dv(50) = 37.8 μm, and Dv(90) = 60.7 μm.

stage_name_raw: PBF-LB fabrication of α–β Ti-O-Fe specimens
stage_goal: Fabricate dense, near-net-shape specimens with fine equiaxed prior-β grains and ultrafine α–β lamellae using optimized laser parameters.
stage_input: optimized processing window (VED, laser power, scanning speed, hatch spacing)
stage_output: as-printed Ti-0.45O-4Fe plate specimens (40 mm × 40 mm × 10 mm)
as-printed Ti-0.5O-5Fe cylindrical specimens (φ9 mm × 80 mm)

evidence.text:
PBF-LB fabrication
A commercial Bright Laser Technologies (BLT, Xi’an, China) S210/S200 system, with a laser spot size of 60/80 μm and a wavelength of 1060–1080 nm, was utilized for the PBF-LB fabrication. The system offers a maximum laser power of 500 W and a maximum scanning speed of 7000 mm/s.

We printed 22 plate specimens (40 mm × 40 mm × 10 mm) of the Ti-0.45O-4Fe alloy in two batches (Supplementary Fig. 5c), and 36 cylindrical specimens (φ9 mm × 80 mm) of the Ti-0.5O-5Fe alloy in a single batch.

stage_name_raw: Post-PBF-LB annealing to optimize microstructure and eliminate metastable phases
stage_goal: Select optimal annealing temperature (800 °C for Ti-0.45O-4Fe; 900 °C for Ti-0.5O-5Fe) to eliminate ω-phase, relieve residual stresses, stabilize α–β lamellar structure, and minimize dislocation density while maintaining coherent interfaces and desired lamellar thickness.
stage_input: annealing furnace with vacuum quartz tube

evidence.text:
Post-PBF-LB annealing treatments
To eliminate metastable phases, relieve residual stresses, and achieve a stable lamellar α−β structure, we annealed our PBF-LB-fabricated Ti-0.45O-4Fe alloy plate samples at 600 °C, 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C for 1 h each, where the β-transus temperature of our alloy is predicted to be 910 °C using the JMatPro 7.0 software.
At 600 °C, the ω-phase persisted (Supplementary Figs. 8, 9), whereas annealing at ≥800 °C eliminated it (Supplementary Fig. 8).

Annealing at 800 °C for 1 h yielded a RT microstructure containing 22 vol.% β-phase... JMatPro simulations predicted a negligible oxygen content in the β-phase (0.001% at 800 °C), thereby concentrating the oxygen in the α-phase to approximately 0.58%.

stage_name_raw: Quasi-static tensile testing to evaluate mechanical properties
stage_goal: Experimentally measure yield strength (σ0.2), uniform elongation (εUEL), and total elongation (εf) to validate achievement of target properties.
stage_input: Instron 5848 machine with 2 kN load cell and non-contact laser extensometer

evidence.text:
Mechanical testing
Tensile testing. Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests were conducted using an Instron 5848 machine equipped with a 2 kN load cell and a non-contact laser extensometer at RT.

The resulting high-strength α–β alloys achieve record uniform elongations: Ti-0.45O-4Fe delivers ≥14% (total: ≥27%) at yield strengths ≥980 MPa, and Ti-0.5O-5Fe achieves ≥13% (total: ≥23%) at yield strengths ≥1075 MPa.

stage_name_raw: In-situ EBSD and TEM analysis to confirm <c + a> slip activation and interfacial slip transfer
stage_goal: Validate the mechanistic basis of the design—activation of {11̅22}<c + a> slip and its transfer across α–β interfaces—using in-situ tensile testing coupled with electron microscopy.
stage_input: tensile specimens subjected to in-situ SEM/EBSD and TEM
EBSD phase maps, TEM g·b analysis, KAM mapping
stage_output: slip transfer statistics (e.g., 57% of events mediated by {11̅22}<c + a>)

evidence.text: To understand the advanced uniform plasticity in high-oxygen Ti-0.45O-4Fe alloy, we performed in-situ EBSD tensile testing, focusing on the uniform deformation stage (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 18). The analysis revealed activation of both prismatic and pyramidal slip (Supplementary Fig. 19), with a distribution of 20% for {10̅10}<a>, 24% for {10̅11}<a>, and 52% for {11̅22}<c + a>.

TEM analysis of the Ti-0.45O-4Fe alloy annealed at 800 °C for 1 h and tested to 14.2% uniform elongation revealed abundant dislocations in both α and β phases within the uniformly deformed region (Fig. 5c–f) and the necking zone (Supplementary Fig. 21). Two-beam TEM g·b analysis confirmed the predominance of <c + a> dislocations in the deformed α phase and revealed distinct slip traces traversing α–β interfaces (Fig. 6), validating our <c + a>-dislocation-centered design strategy.

stage_name_raw: Dilatometric measurement of sintering behavior at multiple heating rates
stage_goal: Acquire experimental relative density vs. temperature data at different heating rates (2.5, 10, and 25°C min−1) to construct the master sintering curve.
stage_output: dilatometric density curves vs. furnace temperature

evidence.text: The MSC was determined by the dilatometric method using a horizontal Linseis L75 dilatometer equipped with an alumina measurement system. The dilatometric behavior was evaluated at different heating (2.5, 10, and 25◦C min−1) in air.

stage_name_raw: Fitting Boltzmann function to dilatometric data to extract master sintering curve
stage_goal: Derive the master sintering curve (MSC) by minimizing deviation of experimental Θ(T,t)–ρ data from a Boltzmann fitting function and determining optimal activation energy Q.

evidence.text: The MSC was determined by minimizing the deviation of the experimental data in the Θ(T,t) −ρplane from a fitting Boltzmann function.
The best result, minimizing the error (inset in Figure 2B), was obtained assuming an activation energy for densification of 650 kJ mol−1.
evidence.section: 3.1 Identification of the master sintering curve

stage_name_raw: Preparation of green pellets and application of three sintering protocols
stage_goal: Generate candidate sintered samples under three distinct thermal schedules: (i) conventional sintering (10°C min−1), (ii) fast firing with 120 min dwell, and (iii) fast firing with 10 min dwell.
stage_output: sintered pellets for each protocol (two per condition)

evidence.text: Cylindrical pellets (diameter = 13 mm, thickness ≈2 mm) were shaped by uniaxially pressing 3YSZ granulated powder (TZ-3YB-E, Tosoh Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) under 220 MPa using a steel die. The green pellets were debinded at 600◦C for 30 min in a muffle furnace (Nabertherm GmbH) under a static air atmosphere... The debinded samples were then subjected to three different sintering procedures using a Nabertherm GmbH muffle furnace operating in static air: (i) conventional sintering using 10◦C min−1 as heating and cooling rate and 120 min isothermal-dwell at different temperatures; (ii) FF with 120 min dwell and (iii) FF with 10 min dwell at the sintering temperature.

stage_name_raw: Finite element modeling of sample thermal history during fast firing
stage_goal: Compute actual temperature evolution inside the pellet during fast firing to accurately calculate Θ(T,t) integral, accounting for furnace temperature drop and sample heating dynamics.
stage_input: pellet thermal conductivity and specific heat
stage_output: FEM-simulated temperature curve at pellet center
corrected Θ(T,t) values for FF experiments

evidence.text: Two finite elements method (FEM) simulations were performed using the COMSOL multiphysics software... The time needed to heat up the sample as it were introduced in the hot furnace at the equilibrium is in the order of ≈7 s according to FEM (Figure 4B). On the other hand, when opening the furnace to introduce the pellets for FF the furnace temperature immediately dropped ≈40◦C and reach again the nominal value in ≈1–1.5 min. evidence.section: 3.3 Fast firing versus master sintering curve

stage_name_raw: Comparison of experimental sintering densities against master sintering curve
stage_goal: Evaluate whether fast-fired samples deviate from the MSC predicted by dilatometry—indicating heating-rate-dependent sintering kinetics.

evidence.text: Plotting the relative densities for fast-fired materials together with the MSC helps to reveal the dissimilarities with the conventional behavior.

We can observe a quite good agreement between the sintering experiments and what extrapolated from dilatometry. However, we can also observe that the samples obtained by FF, either 10 min or 120 min, show a slightly improved densification compared to the conventionally fired materials. The difference is in any case modest, typically below 3%.
evidence.section: 3.3 Fast firing versus master sintering curve

stage_name_raw: Characterization of density, porosity, and microstructure across sintering conditions
stage_goal: Experimentally validate sintering outcomes via Archimedes’ density, Hg porosimetry, and SEM microstructural analysis to confirm MSC predictions and assess pore/grain evolution.

evidence.text: The density of the sintered samples was determined by Archimedes’ method using an analytical balance Gibertini (Italy) and deionized water as the buoyancy medium. The samples were prepared using the ASTM C830-00(2016) as a reference. The open pores size and distribution were evaluated by Hg porosimetry (Porosimeter 2000, Carlo Erba, Italy). The microstructure was studied by polishing and thermally etching the sintered samples. Polishing was carried out using SiC papers (up to grit 4000) and 1 μm diamond paste. The thermal etching was carried out at 10◦C min−1 with 30 min dwell at different temperatures which were selected on each sample to avoid variations in Θ > 5%. The microstructure was then observed at the sample center with an FE-SEM (Zeiss Supra40). To make the sample conductive, these were coated with a sputtereted Pt–Pd thin film.

The results show the onset of close pore formation at a relative density of around 85%. The maximum amount of closed pores is achieved when the relative density is around 90%, and then also the closed porosity is removed from the system. The same pathway is followed for all the sintering conditions, that is, conventional sintering 120 min, FF 120 min, and FF 10 min.
evidence.section: 3.2 Density evolution during fast firing and conventional sintering

stage_name_raw: Provenance of Industrially Produced Glasses
stage_goal: To obtain samples from industrial trials carried out in a collaboration between Costain Ltd and Tetronics Technologies Ltd at the Tetronics’ pilot plasma operating facility in Swindon, UK.

evidence.text: The as-trained potential exhibits excellent predictive accuracy and can reliably reproduce the melting point and enthalpy of fusion of HfO2 and ZrO2 , as illustrated in Table S1 . The predicted melting points of HfO2 and ZrO2 are 2875◦C (3148 K) and 2770◦C (3043 K), respectively, agreeing well with experimental measurements [ 3, 23, 24 ] and references therein. The enthalpies of fusion are also consistent with recently measured data [ 25 ]. These agreements indicate the high accuracy of the DP_SCAN model in predicting the melting points.

evidence.text: Based on the DP_SCAN model, we systematically calculated the melting point evolution of HfO2 -based solid solutions with a series of dopant elements (Y3 + , Yb3 + , Lu3 + , Sc3 + , In3 + , La3 + , Ta5 + , Ca2 + ) at doping concentrations ranging from 5 at.% to 30 at.%, with an interval of 5 at.%. stage_name_raw: structural and thermodynamic characterization of bonding effects
stage_goal: To reveal atomic-scale mechanisms (bond compression, RDF peak width, melting enthalpy) linking composition to melting point
stage_output: three-factor framework: synergistic bond strengthening, chemical bond distribution uniformity, charge-compensating defect compatibility

evidence.text: We further establish a unified three-factor framework for melting point regulation in HfO2 , revealing the critical roles of synergistic bond strengthening, chemical bond distribution uniformity, and charge-compensating defect compatibility, which helps rationalize the various melting point regulation behaviors.

Collectively, our results establish a unified three-factor mechanism for melting point regulation in doped HfO2 : (i) synergistic compression and strengthening of both host Hf–O bonds and dopant M–O bonds, the core prerequisite for breaking the solid solution melting point averaging effect; (ii) minimal doping-induced local structural distortion, the necessary precondition to maintain lattice uniformity and high-temperature stability; (iii) compatibility of charge-compensating defects with the fluorite structural topology, the fundamental guarantee for the integrity of the oxygen framework.

stage_name_raw: Steam oxidation experiments
stage_goal: Expose SiCf/SiC tube specimens to controlled steam/air environments at 600, 900, and 1200°C for 10 days.

evidence.text: Steam oxidation experiments were performed using a tube furnace (GSL-1700X, Hefei Kejing Materials Technology Co., Ltd., China) with a tube diameter of 60 mm, and the SiCf /SiC composite specimens were placed in a corundum boat. Initially, the SiCf /SiC composite specimens were heated at a rate of 10◦C/min under an Ar atmosphere to avoid oxidation of the samples during the heating step. When the predetermined temperature (600, 900, and 1200◦C) was reached, the H2 O/air mixture was introduced into the furnace at a pressure of 0.1 MPa, and the specimens were held at temperature for 10 days. Deionized water was fed at a constant rate of 2 mL/min and vaporized before entering the reaction zone, while the air flow rate was maintained at 300 mL/min using a calibrated flow controller. Accordingly, The volume ratio of water vapor to air in the composite gas was precisely controlled at H2 O:air = 8.3:1, and the equivalent flow rate was 40 mm/s.

stage_name_raw: Solid-state synthesis and compositional characterization
stage_goal: Prepare phase-pure samples and verify successful elemental substitution via XRD, CIC, and SEM-EDS.
stage_output: La5Ti6–xTaxO15S3+xCl3–x powders with confirmed S/Cl/Ti/Ta ratios

evidence.text: La5Ti6–xTaxO15S3+xCl3–x (x = 0, 0.5, 0.75, and 1) samples were synthesized via a solid-state reaction with slight modifications to a previously reported method.19 As shown in Figure S1, nearly identical X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns corresponding to the parent oxychlorosulfide phase (x = 0) were observed for all La5Ti6–xTaxO15S3+xCl3–x samples (0 ≤x ≤1); however, the amount of impurity phases (e.g., LaTiTaO6) increased with increasing x.

The substitution of Cl– with S2– altered the sulfur and chlorine contents in the La5Ti6–xTaxO15S3+xCl3–x samples, as determined by combustion ion chromatography (CIC). For each x value, the Cl content was nearly identical to the nominal composition, whereas the S content was approximately 85% of the nominal value (Table S1), indicating that sulfur incorporation was lower than expected from the sulfur species added during sample preparation.

The aliovalent substitution of S2– for Cl– and Ta5+ for Ti4+ was further confirmed by scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS). The constituent elements of La, Ti, (Ta), O, S, and Cl were homogeneously distributed throughout the La5Ti6–xTaxO15S3+xCl3–x samples...

From x = 0 to 0.75, the lattice parameters increased linearly with increasing x because Cl– (181 pm) and Ti4+ (60.5 pm) were substituted with the larger S2– (184 pm) and Ta5+ (64.0 pm) ions...
